knowledge_point.title: Writing an Inhomogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-t\,{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-t\,{x}_{3}+3{x}_{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &=3{x}_{2}-t\,{x}_{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -t\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the Laplace Transformed Solution

question.:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &={x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}=\frac{3}{s+1},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}=-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{4}{s-2}.
$$

Find the solution to the original initial value problem.

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{-t}+\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{2t}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} |  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{1}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3}{s+1}} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}} \\  & =3{e}^{-1\cdot t} \\  & =3{e}^{-t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{2}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{4}{s-2}} \\  & =-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}}+4{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-2}} \\  & =-{e}^{-1\cdot t}+4{e}^{2\cdot t} \\  & =-{e}^{-t}+4{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-t}+4{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution $$ {X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}=\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{s-2},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s-2}. $$ Find the solution to the original initial value problem.
$x(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,+\,\,$ {{field-2}} $\,\,{e}^{2t}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{s-2}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\} \\  & =1+{e}^{2\cdot t} \\  & =1+{e}^{2t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s-2}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\} \\  & =1-{e}^{2\cdot t} \\  & =1-{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+{e}^{2t} \\ 1-{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system is

| $x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$ |  | $-\frac{7}{10}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ -\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-a \\ -b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3b \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-a \\ -b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3b+4 \\ 3a+1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3b+4 &=-a \\ 3a+1 &=-b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
a=3b-4.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
3(3b-4)+1=-b\,⇒\,b=\frac{11}{10}.
$$

So, 

$$
a=3\cdot \frac{11}{10}-4=\frac{33}{10}-\frac{40}{10}=-\frac{7}{10}.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{7}{10} \\ \frac{11}{10}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | ${e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}$ | {{field-1}} |  |

|  | {{field-2}} | ${e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}$ |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t) &={e}^{-2t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-2t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{4t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=0,

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ r(0) &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=1.
$$

- Substituting ${\alpha }_{0}=1$ into the first equation, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}+1={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-6\left(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1)\right)t+1 \\  & =\frac{6}{4}({e}^{-4t}-1)+1 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}({e}^{-4t}-1)+1 \\  & =\frac{-3+3{e}^{-4t}+2}{2} \\  & =\frac{-1+3{e}^{-4t}}{2} \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\left(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1)\right)t \\  & =-\frac{2}{4}({e}^{-4t}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-4t}-1) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4t}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1+3{e}^{-4t} & -3+3{e}^{-4t} \\ 1-{e}^{-4t} & 3-{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-2x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t) &={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(5t) &={e}^{5t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(5t) &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
5t{e}^{5t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}(1-5t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5{e}^{5t}t+{e}^{5t}(1-5t) \\  & ={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{5t}t \\  & =t{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & 3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(4t) &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
3t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $4$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
3{\alpha }_{0}=4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}), \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =3\left(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t})\right)t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((3{e}^{4t}-3{e}^{t})+(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2{e}^{4t}+{e}^{t}),\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}+2{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{4t}-2{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{4t}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{4t}+{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=0,\,{\lambda }_{2}=t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(0) &={e}^{0} \\ r(t) &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=1 \\ t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the first equation, we immediately get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=1.
$$

- Substituting ${\alpha }_{0}=1$ into the second equation, we get

$$
t{\alpha }_{1}+1={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{t}({e}^{t}-1).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\left(\frac{1}{t}({e}^{t}-1)\right)t+1 \\  & =-({e}^{t}-1)+1 \\  & =-{e}^{t}+2 \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & =\left(\frac{1}{t}({e}^{t}-1)\right)t \\  & ={e}^{t}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t}+2 & {e}^{t}-1 \\ 2-2{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1\pm 4\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$ |  | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 8{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & -3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(1+4\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(1-4\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((1+4\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(1+4\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(1+4\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ ({\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+4{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 4t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t+{e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & =-4\cdot \frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1\pm 2\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{-t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(-1+2\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(-1-2\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((-1+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(-1+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(-1+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ (-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{-t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{3t}-({e}^{3t})\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{-4t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-t} \\ -3{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1))} & ={e}^{\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{2}(2) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(1)\end{bmatrix}\right)} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{({J}_{2}(2))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{({J}_{1}(1))}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{({J}_{2}(2))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{1}(1))}.\end{aligned}

$$

| $[$ | $3$ | {{field-1}} | $]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=[$ | $4$ | $].$ |

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2} & -12{y}^{2} \\ 2x & 8y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2} & -12{y}^{2} \\ 2x & 8y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1 \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2} & -12{y}^{2} \\ 2x & 8y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{3}-4{y}^{3}-1 \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3(1)^{2} & -12(1)^{2} \\ 2(1) & 8(1)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}(1)^{3}-4(1)^{3}-1 \\ (1)^{2}+4(1)^{2}-2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & -12 \\ 2 & 8\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x-y & 3{y}^{2}-x \\ 4{x}^{3}-2y & -2x+2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-xy-4 \\ {x}^{4}-2xy+{y}^{2}-5\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.

First, we rewrite the polynomial, interpreting any constants as multiples of the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & ={X}^{2}+4X-5 \\  & ={X}^{2}+4X-5I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(E)={E}^{2}+4E-5I.$

Let's calculate ${E}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{2} & =E\cdot E \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}} ${e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}$
${e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}$ {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-5t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-5t) &={e}^{-5t} \\ r(5t) &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-5t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-10t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10t}({e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{10t}({e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t} & {e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t} \\ {e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t} & {e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |

|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

| $$
\displaystyle x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+\,\,\frac{1}{4}
$$ |  | $8t-14$ |  | . |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{2t}-2{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{-t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t & =(t)\cdot \left(-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}\right)\cdot (1\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{t{e}^{-2t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4}(2t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4}(2t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}12(t-1)-2(2t+1) \\ 24(t-1)-(2t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}8t-14 \\ 22t-25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

| $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,A=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-3}} |  |

and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-2{y}^{′}-3y+{e}^{2t}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}+{e}^{2t}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &=-3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -3 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The third-order differential equation ${y}^{‴}-4{y}^{″}+{t}^{2}{y}^{′}+{e}^{t}y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where

| $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,A=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |  | $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-4}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-5}} | {{field-6}} | {{field-7}} |  |  | {{field-8}} |  |  |  |
|  | {{field-9}} | {{field-10}} | {{field-11}} |  |  | {{field-12}} |  |  |  |

and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t),$ ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t),$ and ${y}^{″}={x}_{3}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=4{y}^{″}-{t}^{2}{y}^{′}-{e}^{t}y+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=4{x}_{3}-{t}^{2}{x}_{2}-{e}^{t}{x}_{1}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &=-{e}^{t}{x}_{1}-{t}^{2}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -{e}^{t} & -{t}^{2} & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={y}^{2}(t)-x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$

| ${u}^{′}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{y}^{2}-x \\ {x}^{2}+2y\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-x)=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2y \\ 2x & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}
$$

given that the general solution to our differential equation is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The solution to the initial value problem is

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{2t}+\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{-t}.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} |  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\ {c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{0} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} &=1 \\ 2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} &=8.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Adding the equations, we get

$$
3{c}_{1}=9\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3+{c}_{2}=1\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-2.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =3\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}\,+\,(-2)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}\,+\,\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm \text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}=\,\,$ |  | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -{\alpha }_{1}t \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\text{i}t) & ={e}^{\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot \text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & =\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $1,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$ |  | $1$ | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $0$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(t) &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
t{e}^{t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}(1-t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3{e}^{t}t, \\ {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{t}t+{e}^{t}(1-t) \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3t \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Identifying the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution of an Inhomogeneous System

question.:question/problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,x(1)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.$*

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | $3(t-1){e}^{2(t-1)}$ |  | $$
\displaystyle \,\,+{\int }_{1}^{t}\,\,
$$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,\text{d}s$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} |  |  | $0$ |  |  |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-1)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3(t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{2(t-1)}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}3(t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{2(t-1)}\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{1}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=4x-2xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-3y+5xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x-2xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-2xy)=4-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+5xy)=5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+5xy)=-3+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}4-2y & -2x \\ 5y & -3+5x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}4-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 5(0) & -3+5(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model

question.:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=0.7x-0.35xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-0.4y+2xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.2,\,2]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=0.7x-0.35xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-0.4y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0.7x-0.35xy)=0.7-0.35y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(0.7x-0.35xy)=-0.35x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.4y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.4y+2xy)=-0.4+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}0.7-0.35y & -0.35x \\ 2y & -0.4+2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}0.7-0.35(2) & -0.35(0.2) \\ 2(2) & -0.4+2(0.2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -0.07 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & -0.07 \\ 4 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-4\cdot (-0.07) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.28 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.2\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

question.:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given the matrices $A$ and ${e}^{At}$ above, compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}).$

| $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At})=A\,{e}^{At}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & =A\,{e}^{At} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case

question.:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=3x(1-0.3x)-4xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-y+xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is 
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=3x(1-0.3x)-4xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=3-1.8x-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=-4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+xy)=-1+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}3-1.8x-4y & -4x \\ y & -1+x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}3-1.8(0)-4(0) & -4(0) \\ 0 & -1+0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=4x(1-5x)-xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-5y+10xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.2,\,0]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is 
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x(1-5x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-5y+10xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-5x)-xy)=4-40x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-5x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-5y+10xy)=10y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-5y+10xy)=-5+10x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}4-40x-y & -x \\ 10y & -5+10x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}4-40(0.2)-0 & -0.2 \\ 10(0) & -5+10(0.2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -0.2 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-y+2xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.5,\,0.5]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is 
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=x(1-x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(1-x)-xy)=1-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}1-2x-y & -x \\ 2y & -1+2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.5 \\ 0.5\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}1-2(0.5)-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 2(0.5) & -1+2(0.5)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-0.5-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-0.5-\lambda )(-\lambda )-1(-0.5) & =0 \\ \lambda (0.5+\lambda )+0.5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5\lambda +0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-0.25\pm 0.25\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{10} \\ 2\sqrt{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

U=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{3}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$
