knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-6y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=6x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\, \\ \,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Block

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{4}(1))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-3}} | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda =1.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{4}(1)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(1) \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} & -\frac{1}{{1}^{2}\cdot 2} & \frac{2}{{1}^{3}\cdot 6} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} & -\frac{1}{{1}^{2}\cdot 2} \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{1} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{cos}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\pi )\right)=\,\,
$$ |  | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | {{field-4}} | $0$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $0$ |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(\pi )\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi ))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right)\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(\pi ),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\pi )) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\pi )\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(\pi )\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right)\,⊕\,\operatorname{cos}⁡({J}_{1}(\pi )) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{tan}⁡\left({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right)=\,\,
$$ |  | $0$ | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $2$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\left({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right)\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={\sec }^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{\sec }^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {\sec }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{\sec }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & {\sec }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\left({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right) & =\left({J}_{1}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right)\,⊕\,\left({J}_{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system is

| $x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $-1$ |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$

$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2a+b+8 &=-5a \\ 2b+7 &=-5b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get 

$$
2b+7=-5b\,⇒\,b=-1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $a,$ we have

$$
2a+(-1)+8=-5a\,⇒\,a=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ -8 & 11\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}-3t-12 \\ -8t-8\end{bmatrix}
$$

The complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system is

| $x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,t+\,\,$ |  | $-25$ |  | . |

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-3t-12 \\ -8t-8\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ -8 & 11\end{bmatrix}\left(\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\right)+\begin{bmatrix}-3t-12 \\ -8t-8\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9({a}_{1}t+{b}_{1})+12({a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}) \\ -8({a}_{1}t+{b}_{1})+11({a}_{2}t+{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3t-12 \\ -8t-8\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0t+{a}_{1} \\ 0t+{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(-9{a}_{1}+12{a}_{2}-3)t+(-9{b}_{1}+12{b}_{2}-12) \\ (-8{a}_{1}+11{a}_{2}-8)t+(-8{b}_{1}+11{b}_{2}-8)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-9{a}_{1}+12{a}_{2}-3 &=0 \\ -8{a}_{1}+11{a}_{2}-8 &=0 \\ -9{b}_{1}+12{b}_{2}-12 &={a}_{1} \\ -8{b}_{1}+11{b}_{2}-8 &={a}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first two equations, we get 

$$
{a}_{1}=21,\,{a}_{2}=16.
$$

 
Substituting these into the third and fourth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we have

$$
{b}_{1}=-25,\,{b}_{2}=-16.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}21 \\ 16\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}-25 \\ -16\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
A  linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation. Given that $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}$ and $T(v)=\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 20\end{bmatrix},$ what is the standard matrix $T$ of $T?$

| $T=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =5\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =5v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=5v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=5.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}=-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{2}{s},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}=\frac{2}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s}.
$$

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |  |

To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{1}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{2}{s}} \\  & =-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}}+2\,{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & =-{e}^{-1\cdot t}+2\cdot 1 \\  & =2-{e}^{-t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{2}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s}} \\  & =2\,{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+1}}-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-2}}-2\,{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & =2{e}^{-1\cdot t}-{e}^{2\cdot t}-2 \\  & =2{e}^{-t}-{e}^{2t}-2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2-{e}^{-t} \\ 2{e}^{-t}-{e}^{2t}-2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So,

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=2x(t)+2,\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

| $\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |

question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,y=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Given the matrices above, write $A{x}^{T}⊙(y+{x}^{T})$ as a matrix product.
$A{x}^{T}⊙(y+{x}^{T})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
$0$ $5$ $4$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Hadamard product of two compatible vectors $u$ and $v$ can be expressed as the matrix product

$$
v⊙u=\text{diag}(v)u.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A{x}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
y+{x}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that they are of the same size; hence, their Hadamard product is well-defined. We conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}A{x}^{T}⊙(y+{x}^{T}) & =\text{diag}(A{x}^{T})(y+{x}^{T}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}14 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

| ${e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))}=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))} & ={e}^{\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}(3) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(0)\end{bmatrix}\right)} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{({J}_{1}(3))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(3),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(3)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3}\end{bmatrix} \\ .\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(0),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(0)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(0) & {f}^{′}(0) & \frac{{f}^{″}(0)}{2} \\ 0 & f(0) & {f}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & 0 & f(0)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{0} & {e}^{0} & \frac{{e}^{0}}{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{0} & {e}^{0} \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{0}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))} & ={e}^{({J}_{1}(3))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{3}(0))} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}-3{t}^{2}+4t-4 \\ -{t}^{2}-2t+1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}t+2 \\ t+1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system is

| $x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+\,\,$ |  | $1$ |  | $\,\,{t}^{2}+\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,t+\,\,$ |  | $1$ |  | . |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} |  |  | $2$ |  |  | {{field-3}} |  |  |  |  |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-3{t}^{2}+4t-4 \\ -{t}^{2}-2t+1\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\left(\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\right)+\begin{bmatrix}-3{t}^{2}+4t-4 \\ -{t}^{2}-2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2({a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1})-({a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}) \\ {a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3{t}^{2}+4t-4 \\ -{t}^{2}-2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-3){t}^{2}+(2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4)t+(2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}-4) \\ ({a}_{1}-1){t}^{2}+({b}_{1}-2)t+({c}_{1}+1)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-3 &=0 \\ 2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4 &=2{a}_{1} \\ 2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}-4 &={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{1}-1 &=0 \\ {b}_{1}-2 &=2{a}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+1 &={b}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the fourth equation and then substituting the corresponding values ​​into the first and fifth equations to solve for ${a}_{2}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get 

$$
{a}_{1}=1,\,{a}_{2}=-1,\,{b}_{1}=0.
$$

 

We substitute these into the second equation to solve for ${b}_{2},$ and then into the sixth and third equations to solve for ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ We finally get

$$
{b}_{2}=2,\,{c}_{1}=-1,\,{c}_{2}=-2.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -\,{t}^{2}+2t-2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 6 & -6\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,y=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.

Given the matrices above, write the following expression as a Hadamard product. Here $(\,\cdot \,)$ denotes matrix multiplication.

| $(AB)\cdot (By)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $⊙$ |  | {{field-2}} |  |  |

|  | $-6$ |  |  | $4$ |  |  |  |  |

The Hadamard product of two compatible vectors $u$ and $v$ can be expressed as the matrix product

$$

$$

In our case, we have

$$
AB=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 6 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
By=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}(AB)\cdot (By) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\text{diag}\left(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}\right)\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}⊙\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((3\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(3\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(3\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{t}}{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{3{e}^{t}-{e}^{3t}}{2}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{t}}{2t}\cdot t+\frac{3{e}^{t}-{e}^{3t}}{2} \\  & ={e}^{t} \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =3\cdot \frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{t}}{2t}\cdot t+\frac{3{e}^{t}-{e}^{3t}}{2} \\  & ={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below. Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to $$ {{field-3}}. $$ Choosing ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by: | | | {{field-4}} | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | | {{field-5}} | | | | | | ${x}_{3}$ | | | that we can rewrite as $$ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Since the two linearly independent solutions are already mutually orthogonal, we only need to normalize them. question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{2}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & 0 & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-x(t)+2{y}^{2}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-4x(t)+{x}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-x+2{y}^{2} \\ -4x+{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x+2{y}^{2})=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x+2{y}^{2})=4y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x+{x}^{2})=-4+2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x+{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4y \\ -4+2x & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4(0) \\ -4+2(0) & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$$
\displaystyle \text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-2x+3y+3 \\ -4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+3y+3)=2x-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+3y+3)=3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5)=-4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5)=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x-2 & 3 \\ -4 & 4y-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(2)-2 & 3 \\ -4 & 4(-1)-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -4 & -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -4 & -5\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=0.8x-0.4xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-0.3y+1.2xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.25,\,2]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=0.8x-0.4xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-0.3y+1.2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0.8x-0.4xy)=0.8-0.4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(0.8x-0.4xy)=-0.4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.3y+1.2xy)=1.2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.3y+1.2xy)=-0.3+1.2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}0.8-0.4y & -0.4x \\ 1.2y & -0.3+1.2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.25 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}0.8-0.4(2) & -0.4(0.25) \\ 1.2(2) & -0.3+1.2(0.25)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -0.1 \\ 2.4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & -0.1 \\ 2.4 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-2.4\cdot (-0.1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.2\sqrt{6}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4y(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(3) \\ y(3)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-3)}\,x(3) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4(t-3)} & (t-3){e}^{4(t-3)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-3)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,-{e}^{4(t-3)}\, \\ \,0\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution $$ {X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}=\frac{3}{s}+\frac{2}{s-3},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}=\frac{3}{s}-\frac{1}{s-3}. $$ Find the solution to the original initial value problem.

To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3}{s}+\frac{2}{s-3}\} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\}+2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-3}\} \\  & =3\cdot 1+2{e}^{3\cdot t} \\  & =3+2{e}^{3t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3}{s}-\frac{1}{s-3}\} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-3}\} \\  & =3\cdot 1-{e}^{3\cdot t} \\  & =3-{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3+2{e}^{3t} \\ 3-{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)$ $\displaystyle \,\,+{\int }_{0}^{t}\,\,$ ${e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))$ $\,\,\text{d}s$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=3x(1-2x)-xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-3y+4xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=3x(1-2x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=3-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+4xy)=-3+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}3-12x-y & -x \\ 4y & -3+4x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}3-12(0.5)-0 & -0.5 \\ 4(0) & -3+4(0.5)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -0.5 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}1-0.4(0)-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 0 & -3+0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=6y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-6x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(3) \\ y(3)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
% Explanation
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-3)}\,x(3) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3))\, \\ \,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3))\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ t\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+\,\,\frac{1}{9}$ {{field-1}} .
$-3t-1$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}4t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 4t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =4t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t} \\  & =4{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}\right)\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}36(t-1)-(3t+1) \\ -(3t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}33t-37 \\ -3t-1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}7{e}^{-t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 7{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{-4t} & -{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-{e}^{2t})-3{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{-4t}}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{2t} \\ -{e}^{-4t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{2t} \\ -{e}^{-4t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{4t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-2t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{4t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-2t} & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{3}{e}^{5t} \\ \frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{3}{e}^{5t} \\ \frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int \frac{7}{3}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{15}{e}^{5t} \\ -\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{-4t} & -{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{15}{e}^{5t} \\ -\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{e}^{t} \\ \frac{9}{5}{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ \frac{9}{5}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=7y(t)+7 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-7x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}{e}^{t}-0\cdot {e}^{t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{e}^{3t} \\ 4{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-2{e}^{3t} \\ 4{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -2{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 4{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{-2}{3}{e}^{3t} \\ -4{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -6 \\ 9 & -8\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}-\,\,\frac{1}{4}$ {{field-1}} .
$90t+45$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-5t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-5\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-5t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-5\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=15t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=15\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =15t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 15\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}+\int 15{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}-15{e}^{-t} \\  & =-15{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ -15{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}10(1-2t)-60(t+1) \\ 15(1-2t)-60(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}80t+50 \\ 90t+45\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=2x(1-x)-2xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-2y+3xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=2x(1-x)-2xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-2y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=2-4x-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x(1-x)-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}2-4x-2y & -2x \\ 3y & -2+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4(0)-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 3(0) & -2+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t)+{y}^{2}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)-5y(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$ and $$
\displaystyle \text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}4x+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-5y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+{y}^{2})=4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-5y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-5y)=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2y \\ 2x & -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $$
\displaystyle {x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t)+y(t)+2 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4y(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$0$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$ and $$
\displaystyle g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$ and $$
\displaystyle g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},

Let's evaluate each part separately:

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
