knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=-0.5x+0.5xy \\ {y}^{′} &=y-5xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.2,\,1]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-0.5x+0.5xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=y-5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=-0.5+0.5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=0.5x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-5xy)=1-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5+0.5y & 0.5x \\ -5y & 1-5x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $$
\displaystyle {x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5+0.5(1) & 0.5(0.2) \\ -5(1) & 1-5(0.2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.1 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -5 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-5)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.5\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}-2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={e}^{2\cdot t}-2\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{2t}-2 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{2}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{3}{s}\} \\  & =-2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-3}\}+3\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =-2{e}^{2\cdot t}+{e}^{3\cdot t}+3\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{3t}-2{e}^{2t}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}-2 \\ {e}^{3t}-2{e}^{2t}+3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}3t \\ t\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+\,\,\frac{1}{3}$ {{field-1}} .
$3(t-1)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3t \\ t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-0}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3t \\ t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(t-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3t-1 \\ 3(t-1)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below. From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$ Now, we compute the $1$st column of $U.$ It is given by: | | | {{field-1}} | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ${u}_{1}=\,\,$ | | {{field-2}} | | | | | | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$ | | | Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to $$ {{field-3}}. $$ Choosing ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by: | | | {{field-4}} | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | | {{field-5}} | | | | | | ${x}_{3}$ | | | that we can rewrite as: $$ \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}}. $$ Next, we orthogonalize ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process to get the corresponding orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Let ${c}_{1}={b}_{1},$ then: | | | {{field-6}} | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ${c}_{2}=\frac{2}{5}\,\,$ | | $1$ | | | | | | {{field-7}} | | | Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$
${u}_{2}=\,\,$ {{field-8}}

{{field-9}}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\begin{bmatrix}-2\sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{(-1)}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}^{f(t)},\,Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.
${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)=\,\,$ $-{e}^{-4t}$ $\,,\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=\,\,$ $\frac{5}{4}$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{4t}\cdot (-2{e}^{2t})-0\cdot {e}^{2t}}\begin{bmatrix}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{-6t}}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -2{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4} \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}. $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$ $-1$
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-3{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ -3\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3a \\ -3b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2b \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3a \\ -3b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2b+1 \\ 2a+5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2b+1=-3a \\ 2a+5=-3b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
-2b+1=-3a\,⇒\,a=\frac{2b-1}{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
2\left(\frac{2b-1}{3}\right)+5=-3b\,⇒\,4b-2+15=-9b\,⇒\,b=-1.
$$

So,

$$
a=\frac{2(-1)-1}{3}=\frac{-2-1}{3}=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the functions $y:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3},$ defined by $$ y(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,f(y)=\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1}{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at $$ \displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}? $$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
$-4$ {{field-3}}
$2$ $-2$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{2} & {y}_{1} \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}-1\cdot 1 \\ -1-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} & {x}_{1} \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ -4 & 4 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{bmatrix} $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+\,\,$ $1$ $\,\,{t}^{2}+\,\,$ $2$ $\,\,t+\,\,$ {{field-1}} .
{{field-2}} {{field-3}} $1$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-({a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}) \\ {a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(-{a}_{2}+2){t}^{2}+(-{b}_{2}+1)t+(-{c}_{2}+3) \\ ({a}_{1}-1){t}^{2}+({b}_{1}+2)t+{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding coefficients of like powers of $t,$ we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{a}_{2}+2=0 \\ -\,{b}_{2}+1=2{a}_{1} \\ -\,{c}_{2}+3={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{1}-1=0 \\ {b}_{1}+2=2{a}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}={b}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first and fourth equations, we get

$$
{a}_{2}=2,\,{a}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting these into the second and fifth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get

$$
{b}_{2}=-1,\,{b}_{1}=2.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the functions $y:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\ {x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\,f(y)=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}_{1}+4{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at $$ \displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}? $$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
$20$ {{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}+4{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}+4{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 2{y}_{1} & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\ {1}^{2}-{0}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & 0 \\ 20 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the functions $y:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\,f(y)=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}_{1}{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{3}\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at $$ \displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}? $$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} $0$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{y}_{2} & 2{y}_{1} \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2} & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}2(1) \\ 3(-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 4 \\ 12 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(2{x}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(2{x}_{1}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(3{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(3{x}_{2}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 4 \\ 12 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -24 \\ 24 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Function

question.:question/problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}x $$ with respect to $x$ at $$ \displaystyle x={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}. $$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2+1+1 \\ 1+2-2 \\ 1-2+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}x $$ with respect to $x$ at $$ \displaystyle x={\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}. $$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4-3 \\ 3+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}. $$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $2\pm 3\text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$
{{field-2}} $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(2+3\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(2-3\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((2+3\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(2+3\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(2+3\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ (2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+{e}^{2t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:

$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0+0 \\ 0+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{3\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
$0$ $-35$
$0$ {{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{3}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{3}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}\left(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y\right)=y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{3}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -7 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -5 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -70 \\ 0 & -35 \\ 0 & 63\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $20$
{{field-2}} $36$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}{x}_{j}..\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $2$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=2y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =2y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =2(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =2\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =2\left(\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 20 \\ -18 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 3}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=(2Ax-b)^{T}(2Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 10 \\ -5\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $-240$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}} $-2140$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=2Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=2Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}=2{\sum }_{j=1}^{3}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=2{x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot 2{x}_{j} \\  & =4{y}_{i}{x}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

 The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $4$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=4y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

 Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =4y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4(2Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4\left(2\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 10 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 & 10 & -5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 110\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 & 10 & -5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}48 \\ 428\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 & 10 & -5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}480 & 480 & -240 \\ 4280 & 4280 & -2140\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}} ${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$
${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$ {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(-2) \\ y(-2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t+2)}\,x(-2) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5(t+2)) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t+2)) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t+2)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5(t+2))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(5(t+2))\, \\ \,\operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t+2))\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhomogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$ and $$
\displaystyle g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the functions $y(x)=Ax$ and $f(y)=By,$ where $x\in {R}^{2},y\in {R}^{3},$ and the matrices $A$ and $B$ are given by $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[0,\,1]^{T}?$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
$11$ {{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{3}$ by multiplying it by $B$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}=B.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 15 \\ 11 & 15\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the functions $y:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,f(y)=\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at $$ \displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}? $$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
$38$ {{field-4}} $34$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2{y}_{1} & 2{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 2+1 \\ 3+2\cdot 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 14 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} & {x}_{1} & 1 \\ 1 & {x}_{3} & {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 14 & 10\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 38 & 52 & 34\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 2 & 3{y}_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}0-{1}^{3} \\ -1\cdot 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3{x}_{1}^{2} & 1 \\ -{x}_{2} & -{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},

question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0+2 \\ 0-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{2}(t)-4,\end{aligned}\right.\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution $$ {X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}=\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}=\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s}. $$ Find the solution to the original initial value problem.
$x(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =2{e}^{2\cdot t}-{e}^{4\cdot t}+1 \\  & =-{e}^{4t}+2{e}^{2t}+1 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={e}^{4\cdot t}+1 \\  & ={e}^{4t}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{4t}+2{e}^{2t}+1 \\ {e}^{4t}+1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,x(1)=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ $3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1))$ $\displaystyle \,\,+{\int }_{1}^{t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,\text{d}s$
{{field-2}} $-{e}^{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$
\displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -{e}^{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{1}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -{e}^{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=(4Ax-5b)^{T}(4Ax-5b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $832$
$0$ {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=4Ax-5b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=4Ax-5b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}=4{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-5{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=4{x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot 4{x}_{j} \\  & =8{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $8$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=8y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =8y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =8(4Ax-5b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =8\left(4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =8\left(\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ -16\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ 15\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}208 \\ -248\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 832 \\ 0 & -992\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution $$ {X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}=\frac{2}{s-2},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}=-\frac{2}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s-5}. $$ Find the solution to the original initial value problem.
$x(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,{e}^{2t}+\,\,$ {{field-2}} $\,\,{e}^{5t}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}

To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{s-2}\} \\  & =2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\} \\  & =2{e}^{2\cdot t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{2}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s-5}\} \\  & =-2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-5}\} \\  & =-2{e}^{2\cdot t}+{e}^{5\cdot t} \\  & =-2{e}^{2t}+{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{2t}+{e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{3}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{3}{4}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -\frac{3}{4} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\sqrt{3}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{3} \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

$$
\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,

$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=2(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 10\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$ $760$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}} $-40$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=2{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}(2{y}^{T}y)=4y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=4{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i}.
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $4$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x,$ so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=4y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =4y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 & 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 & 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}76 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 & 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}760 & 760 \\ -40 & -40\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating Functions Defined Using Matrices

question.:question/problem:
Consider the functions $y(x)=Ax$ and $f(y)=By,$ where $x\in {R}^{3},y\in {R}^{2},$ and the matrices $A$ and $B$ are given by $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[2,\,-1,\,1]^{T}?$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $6$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}} $2$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $B$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}=B.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Function

question.:question/problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}x $$ with respect to $x$ at $$ \displaystyle x={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}. $$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -4 \\ -4 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -4 \\ -4 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4+0-3 \\ -3+0+2 \\ -3+0+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}x $$ with respect to $x$ at $$ \displaystyle x={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}}^{T}. $$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+0+0 \\ 0+0+0 \\ 1+0+0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{bmatrix}. $$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $-2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{-2t}\,\,$ $1-4t$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}} $1+4t$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-2t)={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}(-2t){\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-2t{e}^{-2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}(1+2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(2t) \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & =-8{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(-8t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1-4t & 2t \\ -8t & 1+4t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(2) \\ y(2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-2)}\,x(2) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(t-2)) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-2)) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-2)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3(t-2))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(t-2))\, \\ \,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-2))\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$
