knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-2x+3xy \\ {y}^{′}=4y-5xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-2x+3xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=4y-5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x+3xy)=-2+3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x+3xy)=3x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4y-5xy)=4-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}-2+3y & 3x \\ -5y & 4-5x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $$
\displaystyle {x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-2+3(0) & 3(0) \\ -5(0) & 4-5(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

knowledge_point.title: Identifying the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution of an Inhomogeneous System

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{6t}\end{bmatrix},\,x(1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ $2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1))$ $\displaystyle \,\,+{\int }_{1}^{t}\,\,$ ${e}^{6s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s))$ $\,\,\text{d}s$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$
\displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{6s}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{6s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ {e}^{6s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{1}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{6s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ {e}^{6s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\displaystyle \,\,+{\int }_{0}^{t}\,\,$ $(t-s){e}^{4t}$ $\,\,\text{d}s$
${e}^{4t}$ {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$
\displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}t{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(t-s){e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}t{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}(t-s){e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-t)={e}^{-t} \\ r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{-t} \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ r(5t)={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+4y(t)-2x(t)-3 \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+3y(t)-3\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$ and 
$$
\displaystyle \text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+4y-2x-3 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3y-3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4y-2x-3)=2x-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4y-2x-3)=4 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3y-3)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3y-3)=-2y+3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x-2 & 4 \\ 2x & -2y+3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $$
\displaystyle {x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(1)-2 & 4 \\ 2(1) & -2(1)+3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}. $$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $4t$
$-4t$ {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & 6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1-4t), \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1-4t & 4t \\ -4t & 1+4t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.
$\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(3{J}_{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x,$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡3x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left({J}_{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\ 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{2}(2) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(2)\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2))\,⊕\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{2}(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(2)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(2),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ \since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(2)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2))\,⊕\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=2x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-2y+4xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.5,\,1]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=2x(1-x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-2y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x(1-x)-xy)=2-4x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+4xy)=-2+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}2-4x-y & -x \\ 4y & -2+4x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $$
\displaystyle {x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4(0.5)-(1) & -(0.5) \\ 4(1) & -2+4(0.5)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -0.5 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 4 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(-\lambda )-4\cdot (-0.5) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-0.5\pm 0.5\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(1) \\ y(1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1))\, \\ \,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix} $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,{t}^{2}+\,\,$ $-1$ $\,\,t+\,\,$ {{field-2}} .
$-1$ {{field-3}} $-2$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\left(\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \left(\frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}}{3}\right)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\left(\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}-18}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}+41}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}-24}{3}\right) \\ \left(\frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+9}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-13}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+15}{3}\right)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding coefficients of like powers of $t,$ we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}-18}{3}=0 \\ \frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+9}{3}=0 \\ \frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}+41}{3}=2{a}_{1} \\ \frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-13}{3}=2{a}_{2} \\ \frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}-24}{3}={b}_{1} \\ \frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+15}{3}={b}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first and second equations, we get

$$
{a}_{1}=2,\,{a}_{2}=-1.
$$

Substituting these into the second and third equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get

$$
{b}_{1}=-1,\,{b}_{2}=3.
$$

Finally, substituting these last two values into the fourth and sixth equations, and solving for ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we have

$$
{c}_{1}=1,\,{c}_{2}=-2.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ -{t}^{2}+3t-2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-1,-4]\times [1,4]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,4]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[-2.5,\,2.5]^{T}.$
${x}_{2}=[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4x & -2y \\ 2x & 2y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}4x & -2y \\ 2x & 2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}4x & -2y \\ 2x & 2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2.5 \\ 2.5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4(-2.5) & -2(2.5) \\ 2(-2.5) & 2(2.5)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2(-2.5)^{2}-(2.5)^{2}-4 \\ (-2.5)^{2}+(2.5)^{2}-8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2.5 \\ 2.5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-10 & -5 \\ -5 & 5\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 4.5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2.5 \\ 2.5\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-10)\cdot 5-(-5)\cdot (-5)}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 5 \\ 5 & -10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 4.5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2.5 \\ 2.5\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{75}\begin{bmatrix}33.75 \\ -33.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2.05 \\ 2.05\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-3,-1]\times [1,3]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}x{y}^{3}-y+7 \\ {x}^{3}-xy+1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $[-1,\,2]^{T},$ and compute the components of the first iteration, rounding your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
$[$ $8$ {{field-1}} $]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=[$ {{field-2}} $]$
{{field-3}} $1$ $-2$
${x}_{1}≈[$ $-2.095$ $]$
{{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{3}-y+7) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{3}-y+7) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-xy+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-xy+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{y}^{3} & 3x{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-y & -x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}{y}^{3} & 3x{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}-y & -x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}x{y}^{3}-y+7 \\ {x}^{3}-xy+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},
$$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}{y}^{3} & 3x{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-y & -x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}x{y}^{3}-y+7 \\ {x}^{3}-xy+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{2}^{3} & 3(-1)(2)^{2}-1 \\ 3(-1)^{2}-2 & -(-1)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}(-1)(2)^{3}-2+7 \\ (-1)^{3}-(-1)(2)+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}8 & -13 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $$
\displaystyle ({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{23}{21} \\ -\frac{19}{21}\end{bmatrix}.
$$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{23}{21} \\ -\frac{19}{21}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{23}{21} \\ -\frac{19}{21}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{44}{21} \\ \frac{23}{21}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-2.095 \\ 1.095\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

$$

$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}(AB)\cdot (By) & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\text{diag}\left(\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\right)\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}⊙\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}+\frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,4{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\frac{4}{3}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{3}{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}-\frac{20}{25}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}=\frac{3}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} & \frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Writing an Inhomogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+{e}^{t}y=t+5$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where
$x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,A=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ {{field-3}}
{{field-4}} {{field-5}} {{field-6}}
and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{y}^{′}-{e}^{t}y+(t+5).
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{x}_{2}-{e}^{t}{x}_{1}+(t+5).
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &=-{e}^{t}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+(t+5)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -{e}^{t} & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ t+5\end{bmatrix}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)+{y}^{2}(t)+2x(t)-3y(t)-1 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=x(t)y(t)-3x(t)+y(t)+1\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$$
\displaystyle \text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-3y-1 \\ xy-3x+y+1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-3y-1)=2x+2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-3y-1)=2y-3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-3x+y+1)=y-3,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-3x+y+1)=x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x+2 & 2y-3 \\ y-3 & x+1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(1)+2 & 2(1)-3 \\ 1-3 & 1+1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Predator Extinction Case

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=6x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-2y+xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=6x(1-x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-2y+xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6x(1-x)-xy)=6-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+xy)=-2+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}6-12x-y & -x \\ y & -2+x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}6-12(0)-0 & -0 \\ 0 & -2+0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=6\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

knowledge_point.title: Writing an Inhomogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}-y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where
$x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,A=\,\,$ $0$ {{field-1}} $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ {{field-2}}
$1$ {{field-3}} {{field-4}}
and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{y}^{′}+y+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{x}_{2}+{x}_{1}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Associative Law

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $ABC$, where $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 3 \\ 5 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2\end{bmatrix}. $$
$ABC=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC=(AB)C=A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, $B$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $2\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding $2$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $3\times 2$ matrix, which will require finding $6$ entries.

So, we find the product $AB$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 3 \\ 5 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $AB$ by $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =(AB)C \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 4 \\ 42 & -28\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1$ and $2.$*
${e}^{At}=\,\,$ $-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t}$ $-2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t}$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{t}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-\left(\frac{1}{t}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t})\right)t \\  & =-({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}) \\  & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{t}-{e}^{2t} & 2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -3 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1$ and $6.$*
${e}^{At}=\,\,\frac{1}{5}$ {{field-1}} $3{e}^{t}-3{e}^{6t}$
$2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{6t}$ {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -3 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(6t) &={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-5t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $6$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
5{\alpha }_{0}=6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{5}(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =3\left(-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{t}-{e}^{6t})\right)t+\frac{1}{5}(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((-3{e}^{t}+3{e}^{6t})+(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3{e}^{t}+2{e}^{6t}) \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\left(-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{t}-{e}^{6t})\right)t+\frac{1}{5}(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((-4{e}^{t}+4{e}^{6t})+(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}+2{e}^{6t} & 3{e}^{t}-3{e}^{6t} \\ 2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{6t} & 2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{6t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -5 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-8$ and $-1.$*
${e}^{At}=\,\,\frac{1}{7}$ {{field-1}} $5{e}^{-8t}-5{e}^{-t}$
{{field-2}} $2{e}^{-8t}+5{e}^{-t}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -5 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & -3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-8t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-8t) &={e}^{-8t} \\ r(-t) &={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-8t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-8t} \\ -t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-7t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{7t}({e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t}).
$$

- Multiplying the second equation by $-8$ and adding to the first one, we get

$$
-7{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=-\frac{1}{7}({e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-6\left(-\frac{1}{7t}({e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t})\right)t-\frac{1}{7}({e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}((6{e}^{-8t}-6{e}^{-t})-({e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}(5{e}^{-8t}+2{e}^{-t}) \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2\left(-\frac{1}{7t}({e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{7}(2{e}^{-8t}-2{e}^{-t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-8t}+2{e}^{-t} & 5{e}^{-8t}-5{e}^{-t} \\ 2{e}^{-8t}-2{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-8t}+5{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=-0.5x+0.25xy \\ {y}^{′} &=0.8y-2xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.4,\,2]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-0.5x+0.25xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=0.8y-2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.25xy)=-0.5+0.25y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.25xy)=0.25x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0.8y-2xy)=-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(0.8y-2xy)=0.8-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5+0.25y & 0.25x \\ -2y & 0.8-2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5+0.25(2) & 0.25(0.4) \\ -2(2) & 0.8-2(0.4)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.1 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -4 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-4)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.2\sqrt{10}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Predator Extinction Case

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=5x(1-x)-2xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-4y+2xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[1,\,0]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=5x(1-x)-2xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-4y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x(1-x)-2xy)=5-10x-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x(1-x)-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4y+2xy)=-4+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}5-10x-2y & -2x \\ 2y & -4+2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}5-10(1)-2(0) & -2(1) \\ 2(0) & -4+2(1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-5\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=2x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-y+2xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. $\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.5,\,1]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=2x(1-x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x(1-x)-xy)=2-4x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}2-4x-y & -x \\ 2y & -1+2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4(0.5)-1 & -0.5 \\ 2(1) & -1+2(0.5)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -0.5 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 2 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(-\lambda )-2\cdot (-0.5) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-0.5\pm 0.5\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Associative Law

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $ABC$, where $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}. $$
$ABC=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC=(AB)C=A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix, $B$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $1\times 3$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $1\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding only $1$ entry, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $2\times 3$ matrix, which will require finding $6$ entries.

So, we find the product $AB$ first: 

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(-1)\cdot 2+5\cdot (-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-17\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $(AB)$ by $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =(AB)\,C \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-17\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-68 & 0 & 34\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial

question.:question/problem:
Consider the matrix $C=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ If $f(X)={X}^{2}-5X+6$, find $f(C).$
$f(C)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the polynomial, interpreting any constants as multiples of the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & ={X}^{2}-5X+6 \\  & ={X}^{2}-5X+6I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(C)={C}^{2}-5C+6I.$

Let's calculate ${C}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 0 \\ -10 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(C):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(C) & ={C}^{2}-5C+6I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 0 \\ -10 & 1\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}+6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 0 \\ -10 & 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}20 & 0 \\ -10 & 5\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16-20+6 & 0-0+0 \\ -10-(-10)+0 & 1-5+6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding a Matrix That Represents a Combination of Three Linear Transformations

question.:question/problem:
Construct the matrix $T$ of the linear transformation $T$ that acts on a vector in ${R}^{2}$ as follows (in the order given):

- It rotates the vector by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians counterclockwise about the origin, then

- stretches the result by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ parallel to the $x$-axis, and finally

- scales the result by a scale factor of $4$ with the center of enlargement at the origin.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T=\,\,$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $P$ be the matrix that represents the rotation, $Q$ be the matrix that represents the stretching, and $R$ be the matrix that represents the scaling. These are given by the following elementary transformation matrices:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,Q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,R=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Hence, the combined transformation can be represented by the matrix $RQP:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =RQP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A linear transformation $T$ represents a stretch along the $x$-axis or $y$-axis. Given that $u=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}$ and $T(u)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T=\,\,$ |  |  |  |  |

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we are told that $T$ represents a stretch along the $x$-axis or $y$-axis.

Comparing the $x$- and $y$-components of $u$ and $T(u),$ we note the following:

- the $x$-components of $u$ and $T(u)$ are the same, while

- the $y$-component of $T(u)$ is $\frac{1}{4}$ times the $y$-component of $u.$

So, we conclude that $T$ represents a stretch of scale factor $\frac{1}{4}$ in the $y$-direction. 

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{4}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Writing an Inhomogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
The third-order differential equation ${y}^{‴}+{t}^{2}\,{y}^{″}+(t-1){y}^{′}-5\sqrt{t}\,y={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where
$x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,A=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}} $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ {{field-4}}
{{field-5}} {{field-6}} {{field-7}} {{field-8}}
{{field-9}} {{field-10}} {{field-11}} {{field-12}}
and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t),$ ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t),$ and ${y}^{″}={x}_{3}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-(t-1){y}^{′}+5\sqrt{t}\,y+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{t}^{2}{x}_{3}-(t-1){x}_{2}+5\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{1}+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &=5\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{1}-(t-1){x}_{2}-{t}^{2}{x}_{3}+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 5\sqrt{t} & -(t-1) & -{t}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ {t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=4$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The third-order differential equation ${y}^{‴}-{e}^{t}{y}^{″}+{t}^{2}{y}^{′}+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where
$x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,A=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}} $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ {{field-4}}
{{field-5}} {{field-6}} {{field-7}} {{field-8}}
{{field-9}} {{field-10}} {{field-11}} {{field-12}}
and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t),$ ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t),$ and ${y}^{″}={x}_{3}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}={e}^{t}{y}^{″}-{t}^{2}{y}^{′}-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}={e}^{t}{x}_{3}-{t}^{2}{x}_{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{t}^{2}{x}_{2}+{e}^{t}{x}_{3}+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡t & -{t}^{2} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{15}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below. From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$ Now, we compute the $1$st column of $U.$ It is given by: | | | {{field-1}} | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ${u}_{1}=\,\,$ | | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | | | | | | {{field-2}} | | | Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to $$ {{field-3}}. $$ Choosing ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by: | | | {{field-4}} | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | | ${x}_{2}$ | | | | | | {{field-5}} | | | that we can rewrite as: $$ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}}. $$ Next, we orthogonalize ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process to get the corresponding orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Let ${c}_{1}={b}_{1},$ then: | | | $1$ | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ${c}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}\,\,$ | | {{field-6}} | | | | | | {{field-7}} | | | Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$
${u}_{2}=\,\,$ $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}$
{{field-8}}
{{field-9}}

{{field-11}}
$\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{3}}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ \sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} \\ -\sqrt{2} \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{2}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+\sqrt{2}{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}-\frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\frac{3}{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given the cubic function $f(x;a,b)=a{x}^{3}+b,$ compute ${∇}_{a,b}\,f.$
${∇}_{a,b}\,f=\text{ }$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute ${∇}_{a,b}\,f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to $a$ and $b.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂a} & =\frac{∂}{∂a}(a{x}^{3}+b)={x}^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂b} & =\frac{∂}{∂b}(a{x}^{3}+b)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{a,b}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂a} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂b}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+xz$, compute ${∇}_{y,z}({∇}_{y,z}\,f).$
${∇}_{y,z}({∇}_{y,z}f)=\text{ }$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the variable subset gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{y,z}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+yz+xz) \\ \frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+yz+xz)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x+z \\ x+y\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the second derivatives with respect to $y$ and $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+z)=0\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}(x+z)=1 \\  & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{y,z}({∇}_{y,z}\,f) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂z} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂y} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{z}^{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1\pm 2\text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$ $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ {{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ {{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(1+2\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(1-2\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((1+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(1+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(1+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ ({\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
